qs.q: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for a new murmur. She has a history of childhood pharyngitis. Which valve is statistically the most frequently affected by rheumatic heart disease?
o: The pulmonic valve affected by rheumatic heart disease
The tricuspid valve affected by rheumatic heart disease
The mitral valve affected by rheumatic heart disease
The aortic valve affected by rheumatic heart disease
qs.e: The mitral valve is the single most commonly affected valve in rheumatic heart disease, followed by the aortic valve. The pulmonic valve is almost never affected.

qs.q: A researcher is studying the molecular mechanisms of rheumatic heart disease following a Group A Streptococcus infection. Which process best describes how streptococcal infection initiates cardiac valve damage?
o: Direct bacterial colonization and destruction of the endocardial endothelium by Staphylococcus
Immune response against streptococcal M-protein cross-reacting with cardiac proteins
Deposition of immune complexes composed of streptococcal toxins directly into the myocardium
Direct toxic injury to the chordae tendineae mediated by extracellular bacterial enzymes
qs.e: Antibodies formed against the M-protein of Group A Streptococcus mistakenly attack cardiac proteins due to molecular mimicry, leading to pancarditis. Staph aureus is more commonly associated with acute infective endocarditis.

qs.q: A patient with chronic rheumatic heart disease undergoes valve replacement surgery. Gross examination of the excised mitral valve reveals fibrosed, fused leaflets with shortened, thickened chordae tendineae, presenting a classic 'fish mouth' appearance. This morphological change is the hallmark of which condition?
o: Severe mitral regurgitation with extensive annular dilation
Fixed mitral stenosis with commissural fusion of the leaflets
Severe aortic regurgitation with calcific cusp retraction
Fixed tricuspid stenosis with fibrous thickening of cusps
qs.e: Leaflet fusion at the commissures giving a 'fish mouth' or 'buttonhole' appearance is the classic gross pathology of mitral stenosis caused by rheumatic heart disease. Regurgitation is typically linked to valve prolapse or incomplete closure rather than fixed commissural fusion.

qs.q: What is the primary pathogenic mechanism responsible for acute rheumatic heart disease following a streptococcal infection?
o: Molecular mimicry involving antibodies to strep M protein
Direct bacterial invasion of the cardiac valve leaflets
Immune complex deposition within renal glomeruli tissue
Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction process
qs.e: Acute rheumatic heart disease arises via molecular mimicry where antibodies directed against group A streptococcal M protein cross-react with host cardiac tissue (Type II hypersensitivity). Direct microbial invasion does not cause the valvular lesions.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease?
o: Rheumatic heart disease is a long-term cardiac complication of acute rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic heart disease is caused by direct bacterial invasion of the heart valves.
Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease represent the exact same acute phase.
Rheumatic heart disease occurs concurrently during the initial pharyngitis episode.
qs.e: Rheumatic heart disease is the late manifestation and long-term consequence of acute rheumatic fever. The acute episode involves inflammation, whereas RHD results from chronic valve damage.

qs.q: What are Anitschkow cells, which are typically found within the granulomas associated with rheumatic heart disease?
o: Enlarged macrophages
Malignant lymphocytes
Necrotic myocytes
Infected neutrophils
qs.e: Anitschkow cells are enlarged macrophages found within granulomas called Aschoff bodies in rheumatic heart disease. Larger Anitschkow cells may coalesce to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells.

qs.q: What epidemiological pattern is most characteristic of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease globally?
o: It is primarily a disease of poverty and low socioeconomic status.
It has the highest incidence rates in wealthy urban centers of the West.
It predominantly affects elderly populations older than 65 years.
It shows an equal distribution across all global regions regardless of crowding.
qs.e: RHD is strongly linked to poverty and low socioeconomic status, where patients often do not seek medical attention when they contract pharyngitis. Developed nations have seen a sharp decline due to improved hygiene and reduced household crowding.

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with chronic rheumatic heart disease. Which of the following heart valves is most commonly affected alone in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
o: Aortic valve
Mitral valve
Tricuspid valve
Pulmonary valve
qs.e: In chronic rheumatic heart disease, the mitral valve alone is the most commonly affected valve, seen in about 50% to 60% of cases. The pulmonary valve, by contrast, is rarely affected.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatic heart disease is an autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis that damages heart valves, especially the mitral and aortic. It presents with murmurs, heart failure, and systemic features of acute rheumatic fever. Early recognition and secondary prophylaxis prevent progression.

sections.p: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is chronic valve damage following acute rheumatic fever (ARF), an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococcal infection. Diagnosis combines clinical criteria (Jones) with echocardiographic evidence of valve lesions.
b: ARF per Jones criteria; echo shows regurgitation or stenosis

t.b: Normal valves rule out RHD; abnormal valves with history of ARF confirm diagnosis

sections.p: RHD is staged by valve involvement and functional class. The World Heart Federation (WHF) echo criteria classify mild, moderate, and severe lesions, guiding treatment urgency.
b: Moderate: two valves or significant stenosis
Severe: critical stenosis or heart failure

t.b: Class I: no limitation; Class IV: symptoms at rest

sections.p: The primary trigger is untreated or inadequately treated group A streptococcal pharyngitis. In low‑resource settings, recurrent infections, poor access to antibiotics, and malnutrition heighten risk.
Patients may have a history of ARF with migratory arthritis, chorea, or carditis. Chronic RHD presents with a systolic murmur, dyspnea, edema, and signs of heart failure.
b: Systolic murmur at apex (mitral regurgitation) or pulmonic area (aortic stenosis)

t.b: Presence of a harsh systolic murmur suggests stenosis

sections.p: Echocardiography is the cornerstone. Blood tests for ASO and CRP support recent infection. In resource‑poor settings, a focused echo or portable device may suffice.

t.b: Thickened leaflets with regurgitation confirm RHD

sections.p: Acute heart failure, arrhythmias, embolic events, and sudden death are life‑threatening complications. Watch for rapid symptom worsening or new murmurs.

t.b: Increased vascular markings indicate heart failure

sections.p: Treat the underlying streptococcal infection, provide secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin, and manage heart failure with diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and beta‑blockers. Surgical valve repair or replacement is reserved for severe cases.

Regular clinical review, echocardiography every 1–2 years, and adherence to monthly penicillin injections are essential. Public health measures include improving sanitation and early treatment of sore throats.
Mitral valve prolapse, infective endocarditis, and congenital valve disease can mimic RHD murmurs.
Low ASO titers may occur in chronic infections; normal CRP does not exclude carditis; echo may miss mild lesions in inexperienced hands.
b: ASO may be low after prolonged infection
CRP can be normal in chronic inflammation

faq.a: Valve damage is irreversible; treatment focuses on preventing progression and managing complications.
It is generally safe; monitor for hypersensitivity reactions.

faq.q: How often should I get an echo?
faq.a: Every 1–2 years in endemic areas; sooner if symptoms change.
